title: MRI Scanner
subtitle: A superconducting magnet, three gradient coils and an RF coil that image the body without opening it
summary: An MRI scanner does not take a photograph. It aligns the hydrogen nuclei in the body with a strong magnetic field, then knocks them out of alignment with a radio pulse. As they relax they emit a signal that depends on the tissue around them. Gradient coils encode position, and a computer turns the signals into slices.

parts.name: Base Skid
parts.short: The frame that spreads the magnet's weight
parts.detail: The magnet weighs several tonnes, so the skid spreads the load across the floor and carries the leveling feet.

parts.name: Magnet Housing
parts.short: The white doughnut around the bore
parts.detail: The housing contains the superconducting coil and its liquid-helium bath. The large white surface is the cryostat's outer cover.

parts.name: Cryostat
parts.short: Keeps the coil at four kelvin
parts.detail: The coil is bathed in liquid helium inside a vacuum vessel. The rings and struts support the cold mass while limiting heat leak.

parts.name: Bore Lining
parts.detail: A smooth plastic liner covers the gradient and RF coils and gives the patient a clear opening.

parts.name: Gradient Coils
parts.detail: Three coil sets create small field gradients along X, Y and Z. Switching them encodes which slice and which pixel each signal comes from.

parts.name: RF Body Coil
parts.short: Transmits the radio pulse and receives the echo
parts.detail: A birdcage coil surrounds the body. It tips the hydrogen nuclei with a radio pulse and then listens for their relaxation signal.

parts.name: Helium Ports
parts.detail: Service ports let engineers fill liquid helium and recover boil-off gas without warming the magnet.

parts.name: Quench Vent
parts.short: Carries away helium in an emergency
parts.detail: If the coil loses superconductivity, the stored energy boils the helium. The quench vent routes the gas safely out of the room.

parts.name: Patient Table
parts.short: Slides the patient into the bore
parts.detail: The table is non-magnetic and locks into the scanner. It positions the region of interest at the centre of the magnet.

parts.name: Table Rails
parts.detail: Rails keep the table aligned with the bore. A drive moves it in precise steps during the scan.

parts.name: Control Console
parts.short: Where the technologist runs the scan
parts.detail: The console holds the controls, display and intercom. The operator selects the sequence and monitors the patient from the adjacent room.

parts.name: Console Screen
parts.detail: The screen displays scout images, slice planning and scan progress.

parts.name: Chiller
parts.short: Removes heat from the gradient coils
parts.detail: Gradient coils produce a lot of heat when switching. A water chiller carries that heat away so the coils stay stable.

parts.name: Coolant Hoses
parts.short: Connect the chiller to the magnet
parts.detail: Flexible hoses carry chilled water to the gradient coil cooling circuit.

parts.name: Bore Light
parts.detail: A ring light around the bore helps the patient and technologist see inside.

parts.name: Nameplate
parts.detail: The plate records the field strength, magnet type and serial number.

steps.title: A field that lines up the nuclei
steps.body: The superconducting magnet produces a strong, uniform field. Hydrogen nuclei in the body align with it, creating a tiny net magnetisation.

steps.title: A radio pulse tips them over
steps.body: The RF coil transmits a pulse at the resonance frequency. The nuclei absorb it and tip away from the field; when the pulse ends they relax back and emit a signal.

steps.title: Gradients encode position
steps.body: The gradient coils make the field slightly stronger in one direction. That changes the resonance frequency with position, so the received signal can be assigned to a slice and a pixel.

steps.title: Heat has to leave
steps.body: Switching gradients quickly generates heat. The chiller and coolant hoses keep the coils at a stable temperature, which keeps the images reproducible.

quiz.prompt: Tap the coil that transmits the radio pulse.
Tap the coils that encode position in three directions.
Tap the part that keeps the magnet cold.
What does an MRI scanner actually detect?
choices: Radio signals from relaxing hydrogen nuclei
quiz.explain: The scanner listens for the radio-frequency signal emitted by hydrogen nuclei as they relax.

quiz.prompt: Why does the gradient coil need a chiller?
choices: To remove heat from the switching coils
quiz.explain: Fast gradient switching produces heat; water cooling keeps the coils stable.
